claims.text: Short-term thermal exposure causes diffusion-driven phase separation in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
The thermally induced phase separation precipitates thermodynamically stable intermetallic compounds.
The newly precipitated intermetallic compounds are enriched in passivating elements.
The newly formed intermetallic phases catalyze formation of an adherent, protective oxide during high-temperature exposure.
The newly formed intermetallic phases reduce localized corrosion in saline environments.
An as-cast Al–Mg–Cu–Zn–Gd or Al–Mgₓ–Ti–Sn–Zn alloy has a mixed microstructure of metastable solid-solution regions and dispersed intermetallic compounds.
Annealing at 500–600 °C for several hours under inert atmosphere permits diffusion-driven phase evolution.
Stable intermetallic precipitates partition Mg, Cu, or Ti into surface and near-surface regions.
Elemental diffusion during annealing transforms the non-equilibrium microstructure through phase separation.
The transformed intermetallic phases alter local chemistry and nucleate a more uniform and adherent oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
The phase transformation reduces micro-galvanic couples that accelerate corrosion.
Annealed material will develop a more homogeneous and adherent oxide scale than the as-cast baseline.
Annealed material will exhibit reduced oxidation weight gain relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealed material will exhibit lower corrosion current density in saline solution than the as-cast baseline.
The as-cast baseline has higher corrosion and oxidation rates than the annealed material.
The proposed mechanism applies to lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³.
Constituent-property differences predispose the relevant alloys to stable-phase formation.
The magnitude and kinetics of the proposed effects vary with alloy composition and thermal-treatment duration.
